title: The Neuroplastic Accessibility Index (NAI): A Hypothesis-Generating Framework for Understanding Intraindividual Variability in Responsiveness to Standard Interventions in Autism
content: Responsiveness to standard interventions in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is often interpreted as reflecting relatively stable individual characteristics. However, clinicians, therapists, educators, and caregivers frequently observe substantial fluctuations in responsiveness within the same individual across time and contexts. While interindividual variability in intervention response has received considerable attention, intraindividual variability remains less clearly explained.This article introduces the Neuroplastic Accessibility Index (NAI), a hypothesis-generating framework that conceptualizes neuroplastic accessibility as distinct from neuroplasticity itself. Whereas neuroplasticity refers to the nervous system’s intrinsic capacity for adaptive change, neuroplastic accessibility refers to the functional availability of biological, physiological, environmental, and behavioral conditions that may support adaptive neuroplastic remodeling at a given time.The framework proposes that neuroplastic accessibility emerges from the dynamic convergence and alignment of four complementary functional requirements: Fuel, representing biochemical-molecular resources; Support, representing physiological and metabolic infrastructure; Trigger, representing appropriately calibrated environmental activation; and Engine, representing behavioral mobilization and engagement. These pillars are hypothesized to influence neuroplastic accessibility and contribute to fluctuations in responsiveness to standard interventions.The NAI further introduces neuroplastic readiness and accessibility-oriented adaptation. Neuroplastic readiness refers to the degree to which specific intervention objectives may currently be accessible. Accessibility-oriented adaptation refers to using readiness information to guide intervention objective selection and identify pillar-specific domains that may benefit from modulation to support future neuroplastic accessibility. Under this framework, accessibility information is not intended to determine whether intervention should occur, but to inform which objectives may be most accessible under current conditions.Although empirical validation remains necessary, the NAI offers a theoretical perspective for understanding intraindividual variability in autism and a translational framework linking neuroplastic accessibility, readiness, adaptation, and future accessibility. It also provides a conceptual foundation for longitudinal monitoring and future digital implementations aimed at characterizing dynamic fluctuations in neuroplastic accessibility over time. More broadly, the NAI may be viewed as a Bio-Psycho-Contextual Readiness perspective, integrating biological, physiological, behavioral, and contextual conditions when evaluating intervention accessibility and adaptive neuroplastic processes.
